evals.prompt: I work for a private company. Basic plus DA is ₹10,00,000 a year. My employer puts ₹1,30,000 a year into my NPS and I put in ₹1,50,000 of my own. What NPS deduction can I claim under the new regime and under the old regime?
expectations: New regime: only the employer contribution is deductible, the full ₹1,30,000 because the limit for every employer is 14% of basic plus DA (₹1,40,000); the own ₹1,50,000 gets no deduction
Old regime: employer contribution limited to 10% = ₹1,00,000; own contribution ₹1,00,000 (10% of salary) under the ₹1.5 lakh limit plus ₹50,000 under the extra 80CCD(1B) amount, total ₹2,50,000
Cites the 14% / 10% split by regime and employer type

evals.prompt: I'm a self-employed consultant with gross total income of ₹12,00,000 and I put ₹2,50,000 into NPS this year. I have no other 80C investments. How much can I deduct if I choose the old regime, and what if I stay in the new regime?
expectations: Old regime: own contribution limited to 20% of gross total income (₹2,40,000) but inside the ₹1.5 lakh limit, so ₹1,50,000 plus the extra ₹50,000, total ₹2,00,000; the remaining ₹50,000 is not deductible
New regime: no deduction for own contributions, and a self-employed person has no employer contribution to claim

evals.prompt: This year my employer contributed ₹4,00,000 to my EPF, ₹3,50,000 to my NPS and ₹1,00,000 to a superannuation fund. Is any of that taxable?
expectations: Adds the three employer contributions (₹8,50,000) and applies the ₹7,50,000 aggregate cap
Treats the ₹1,00,000 excess as a perquisite, plus the annual accretion (interest or returns) on that excess
Says the cap is separate from the 14% or 10% NPS deduction limit
must_not_match: (?i)\bnone of (it|that|this|these)\b[^.]{0,20}\b(is|are) taxable|\bnothing (here )?is taxable|\bno part (of it )?is taxable

evals.prompt: I'm a non-government NPS subscriber retiring with a ₹50 lakh corpus. Under the new PFRDA rules I take 80% as lump sum (₹40 lakh) and put ₹10 lakh into an annuity. How much of the lump sum is tax-free?
expectations: Quotes or applies Schedule II Sl. 6(b): the payment must not exceed 60% of the total corpus (₹30 lakh here); PFRDA's 80% lump sum was not matched by a tax change
Does not call the ₹40 lakh (80%) tax-free: the cautious reading taxes the whole ₹40 lakh; the alternative reading taxes only the ₹10 lakh excess; states which reading it uses or flags the ambiguity
Says buying the annuity is not itself taxed; the pension is taxed when received

evals.prompt: I've contributed ₹8,00,000 of my own money to NPS and my employer has added ₹4,00,000. The corpus is now ₹20,00,000. How much partial withdrawal is tax-free?
expectations: Limits the exempt partial withdrawal to 25% of the subscriber's own contributions, which is ₹2,00,000
Explains that employer contributions and returns are not in the base, so it is not 25% of the corpus (₹5,00,000) or of own plus employer (₹3,00,000)
